claims.text: Protective oxide retention in high-temperature HEAs is governed by inherently sluggish diffusion of key oxide-forming cations.
Sluggish diffusion of Al preferentially produces a dense, slow-growing Al2O3 scale.
A dense Al2O3 scale inhibits further oxygen ingress and thereby improves oxidation resistance.
Al2O3 is a protective high-temperature oxide and grows more slowly than chromium oxide scales.
A standard lower-Al AlCoCrFeNi HEA typically develops non-uniform or less-protective oxide scales at high temperature.
Increasing Al concentration sufficiently will promote formation of Al2O3.
The protective structural mediator is a dense, adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 surface scale.
High configurational entropy in HEAs inherently retards diffusion of metallic species.
In an enhanced-Al alloy, Al diffuses outward more slowly than oxygen diffuses inward.
The proposed imbalance between outward Al diffusion and inward oxygen diffusion causes a continuous protective Al2O3 layer to form.
Lower Al availability in the baseline alloy produces patchy or non-protective scales and faster depletion of Al.
Under identical oxidation conditions, the enhanced-Al HEA will have lower mass gain than the baseline alloy.
Under identical oxidation conditions, the enhanced-Al HEA will develop a more uniform, adherent, Al2O3-dominated scale than the baseline alloy.
Mass gain is an indicator of the extent of high-temperature oxidation.
The proposed mechanism applies in oxygen-rich environments at approximately 900–1100 °C where oxide growth is diffusion controlled.
External coatings or aggressive environmental species can alter the oxidation pathway.
The mass-gain reduction and scale thickness or adherence depend on exact alloy composition and oxidation duration.

contradictions.description: The alloys are described as identical except for Al content, but changing Al concentration necessarily requires changing at least one other elemental fraction unless the composition-normalization or substitution strategy is specified.
